Adult female Plain sculpin reach an impressive ultimate body length of 74 centimeters [Li = 74 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger members of the Cottidae family inhabiting the North Pacific. This maximum recorded total length is attained only after several years of steady growth, during which females accumulate substantial somatic tissue. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for these females is 4313 grams [Wwi = 4313 grams], a mass that reflects the considerable energetic investment required to achieve such dimensions in the cold, productive waters of their benthic habitat. Field surveys indicate that this asymptotic size is rarely observed, as most individuals succumb to predation or senescence before reaching their full growth potential. Nonetheless, the length-weight relationship derived from local populations suggests that the species exhibits a robust, deep-bodied morphology consistent with its demersal lifestyle, where maneuverability along rocky substrates is advantageous for ambushing invertebrate prey.

Puberty in female Plain sculpin is attained at a total length of 47 centimeters [Lp = 47 centimeters], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 1056 grams [Wwp = 1056 grams]. This developmental milestone marks the onset of gonadal maturation and the capacity to participate in seasonal spawning aggregations. The transition from a juvenile, non-reproductive state to a reproductively competent adult is accompanied by distinct shifts in energy allocation, with a greater proportion of ingested resources redirected toward vitellogenesis and gamete production. Individuals typically reach this size threshold during their third or fourth year of life, depending on local food availability and thermal regimes. The body mass at this stage represents approximately one-quarter of the ultimate adult mass, indicating that females continue to invest heavily in somatic growth even after becoming sexually mature, a pattern consistent with an iteroparous life history strategy that prioritizes future reproductive episodes.

At the low ambient temperatures characteristic of its high-latitude environment, approximately 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C], the Plain sculpin exhibits a maximal reproductive output of roughly 780 eggs per female per day [Ri = roughly 780 eggs per female per day], a rate derived from a relative fecundity of 66 eggs per gram of maternal body weight. This calculation assumes a female of ultimate mass contributing daily to the spawning stock over the course of the breeding season. To express this in more biologically intuitive terms, a single gravid female at an asymptotic body mass of over four kilograms (4313 grams) [Wwi = 4313 grams] can produce an estimated annual total of approximately 285,000 eggs, partitioned across multiple spawning events. Each spawning event may release roughly 66 eggs per gram [N_R_i = 66 eggs per gram] of maternal body weight, with several such events occurring each season [F_R_i = several such events occurring each season]. This high fecundity is typical of many marine cottids, which rely on large egg numbers to offset the considerable mortality experienced during the pelagic larval phase. The temperature of 2.4 °C is close to the lower thermal tolerance limit for successful embryonic development, yet it represents the typical winter spawning condition in the species' native range.

Newly hatched Plain sculpin larvae emerge from demersal eggs at a remarkably small size, with an initial wet weight at birth of just 0.0072 grams [Wwb = 0.0072 grams]. This minimal mass, a direct consequence of the egg diameter of approximately 2.4 millimeters, is comparable to that reported for the closely related shorthorn sculpin Myoxocephalus scorpius and reflects the species' reliance on high fecundity rather than large offspring. The yolk-sac larva, or alevin, relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first days post-hatching, before its mouth gape is sufficiently developed to commence exogenous feeding. The transition to active prey capture is a critical bottleneck; larvae that fail to locate suitable microzooplankton within the window of yolk absorption experience irreversible starvation. The lecithotrophic phase is brief, typically lasting no more than a week at the prevailing water temperature of 2.4 °C, after which the prolarva must successfully initiate first feeding to sustain growth and avoid the point of no return.

The maximum lifespan of the Plain sculpin has been estimated at approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years] under natural conditions at a mean annual temperature of 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C]. This longevity is relatively protracted for a cottid of its size, reflecting the slow metabolic rates and reduced predation pressure typical of cold-water, demersal fishes. Senescence becomes apparent in individuals older than a decade, with a noticeable decline in body condition and reproductive output during the final years of life. Comparing the lifespan to the age at puberty reveals that females invest roughly one-third of their total life expectancy in pre-reproductive growth and development, a life-history trade-off that balances the benefits of delayed maturity against the risks of mortality before first reproduction. Field records confirm that very few individuals survive beyond twelve years, with the oldest documented specimen recovered from a trawl survey in the Bering Sea.
